inputs.original_text: The conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran is pushing oil costs upward, and ordinary households and workers will feel the squeeze first—not those with the most wealth or power. Cutting excise duties may steady petrol and diesel prices for now, but it also means less public revenue, with the bill potentially shifted onto people later. This is a reminder that dependence on imported crude leaves India exposed to global shocks. We need an energy system built around resilience and fairness, rather than one that repeatedly makes people already struggling with living costs absorb the consequences.
inputs.modified_text: This is exactly how global crises deepen inequality: households and workers are made to absorb higher costs, while people with the most wealth and power are better placed to ride them out. Cutting fuel duties may offer temporary relief, but if the lost revenue is later recovered through weaker public services or other burdens on ordinary people, that is not a fair solution. India’s dependence on imported crude leaves people vulnerable to shocks they did not cause. We need a just, resilient energy transition that protects workers and low-income households instead of repeatedly asking them to pay the price.
